prize_parts.citation: For the invention and first realisation of the optical lattice clock, and for the development of lattice clocks to the 10^-18 regime of accuracy and stability

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: a single-part prize for optical lattice clocks to Katori and Ye. After the first round I tested it against the strongest objections instead of counting the six supporters, since the chair is right that the opening rankings partly drove the movement. The physical idea is distinct. The magic-wavelength lattice makes the light shift cancel between the clock levels, so thousands of neutral atoms are confined in the Lamb-Dicke regime and probed simultaneously, with Doppler and recoil shifts removed and the statistical noise reduced by the atom number. A comb is a ruler and an ion trap controls one quantum system; neither contains this idea. The result is demonstrated and reproduced: Sr and Yb lattice clocks in Tokyo, Boulder, Paris, Braunschweig and elsewhere have been compared over fibre and free space at the 1e-18 level, and agreement across laboratories is the most convincing evidence I know of that systematic effects are understood. As for a discovery about nature, resolving gravitational redshift across millimetre-scale samples with a single lattice, and many-body effects such as spin-exchange and collective interactions in the clock ensemble, are physics results and not only instrument records. The credit also maps onto the record: Katori for the proposal and the first Sr demonstrations, Ye for taking the lattice clock to the accuracy and stability frontier and for the many-body and comb-linked clock physics. The reasons for these two names should be written into the citation.
statement.case_against: I take three objections seriously. First, novelty relative to 2005 and 2012: a sceptic will say the committee has already told the metrology story twice. I think the magic-wavelength lattice answers this on the science, but I accept that the case is for a new regime of measurement, not a wholly new phenomenon. Second, the fundamental-physics payoff, which Danielsson conditions his support on. From memory and not verified here, the comparisons so far give bounds on drifts of alpha and of mass ratios and on some ultralight dark-matter couplings that are competitive with, and for some quantities better than, other methods, but no deviation has been found. That is a null result, and a prize that rests on it would be weak, so I do not rest the case on it. The case is that a new measurement capability has opened and is already being used. Third, attribution at the edge: Lemonde, Derevianko, Takamoto, Ludlow and the PTB, NIST and SYRTE teams all contributed decisive steps. I cannot find a third person whose claim on the concept is on a par with Katori's, but the citation must say clearly that the credit is for the invention and first realisation and for pushing it to the frontier. A pending SI redefinition and geodesy are not part of my argument for the physics.

responses.point: Danielsson accepts the two-name credit and the distinction from the comb prize, but says a redefinition of the second is a metrological milestone and not a discovery, and wants evidence of competitive bounds on constants or ultralight dark matter before his ballot.
responses.response: I agree that the redefinition of the second is a consequence and not the argument, and I have removed it from my case. On the evidence, my recollection is that lattice-clock and cross-species comparisons have given competitive limits on temporal drift of the fine-structure constant and electron-proton mass ratio, and on some ultralight scalar couplings, but they are null results, so the payoff is as much about reach as about findings. I would not defend the prize as a fundamental-physics discovery, and it should not be cited that way. I would defend it as a discovery-enabling instrument whose first results already constrain physics, and I would ask that the expert reports confirm those bounds from the primary literature, as you request. If they turn out weaker than I recall, I would still keep the clocks first, but the citation should then rest only on the invention and the accuracy frontier and not mention tests of fundamental physics.

responses.point: Mehlig keeps topological insulators first, argues that a new class of quantum matter outweighs a further gain in precision, and says the clock sits close to the 2005 and 2012 prizes with impact beyond metrology still prospective.
responses.response: I accept the principle that a new state of matter weighs heavily, and I think B007 is a very good discovery. I still disagree on the comparison for two reasons. The lattice clock is a new regime of measurement and not just a further gain in precision, because the magic-wavelength condition changes what can be measured, and it has already been used for millimetre-scale redshift and for comparisons across continents. And by your own account the real weak point of B007 is the credit: Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang proposed the HgTe route that Molenkamp's group tested, and Fu, Moore and Hasan are central to the 3D case. A set of three cannot absorb all of them. If you can show how that record is resolved within three names, and how Z2 differs from the 2016 prize beyond conceptual distinction, I would move B007 up. As it stands I keep it as an alternative, and I agree it is a stronger alternative than the others.

responses.point: Olsson wants the citation to say why Katori and Ye are named, with Ye's part anchored in the many-body and comb-linked clock physics and not in accuracy records alone, because a sceptic will call record-setting a later and better experiment.
responses.response: I agree with this and have changed my citation to follow it: it now says invention and first realisation, which is Katori, and development to the 1e-18 regime, which is where Ye's group belongs. I would go one step further and say that for Ye the record is not merely a better version. The 1e-18 level required controlling blackbody radiation shifts, lattice light shifts and atomic interactions in the lattice, and the many-body analysis was a separate scientific advance, with the spin-exchange and collective effects that are now an intrinsic part of the clock design. I would still prefer the citation to be short and not enumerate these, and we can record the reasons for excluding PTB, NIST and SYRTE in the committee's background document and not in the citation. I thank you for flagging that your own first choice B056 should be discounted, and I think that is fair.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks twisted bilayer graphene first, argues that independent confirmation of the phases has been fast and broad, and says he would not oppose B042 if the AMO members find the attribution clean.
responses.response: I appreciate that, and from the AMO side the attribution is as clean as it gets for a field with many strong groups: the magic-wavelength idea and first demonstrations are Katori's, and the frontier performance is documented by independent comparisons. On B054 I do not dispute the speed of confirmation. My concern, which I share with Lindroth and Pearce, is that the superconducting phase and its sensitivity to twist-angle disorder are not yet understood, so the citation would have to be limited to the existence of the phases. That is possible, but it would be for the existence of a platform whose physics is still moving, and the clocks are in the opposite position: the device physics is understood and the open question is where it will be used. I would not oppose B054 if it came to a vote, but I would put it a few years later than the clocks.

responses.point: In round 1 I asked Lindroth whether Zoller's theory is essential to the B010 credit, and she supports a two-name clock credit and distinguishes the ensemble magic-wavelength lattice from single-ion logic.
responses.response: I agree with your distinction between the ensemble lattice and the 2012 single-ion work, and it is the core of the novelty argument I now use in my case. On B010, I remain cautious: the four-name credit exceeds the limit, and the payoff in the 2D Fermi-Hubbard regime is still developing. If the committee prefers a second part in the AMO area, I would not support one this year, because I think a single clean credit is stronger. I keep B010 as an alternative only in case the clocks do not hold up in the final vote.

responses.point: The chair notes that critics may link Ye's comb-linked clock comparisons to Hall and Hansch, and keeps IceCube as a serious alternative to be judged on attribution.
responses.response: I agree that this is where the criticism will come. My answer is that the citation for Ye should lean on the lattice clock and not on comb-linked comparisons, so that the 2005 prize is not reopened. I also keep IceCube in view, but I do not think it should be joined to the clock, for the reasons you and Olsson give: Spiering's role across Baikal and IceCube, and the AMANDA and DUMAND precursors, make two names harder to defend than for the clock.

uncertainties: Whether the primary literature supports the competitive bounds on varying constants and ultralight dark matter that I recall from memory, or whether the fundamental-physics payoff is weaker than I think.
Whether the committee accepts that the magic-wavelength lattice is a distinct idea from the comb and ion-control prizes, or sees the clock as an incremental later step.

Whether the two-name credit can be defended against Lemonde, Derevianko, Takamoto, Ludlow and the PTB, NIST and SYRTE groups, and whether Ye's part is fairly described by the many-body and accuracy-frontier wording in the citation.
Whether the B007 attribution problem (Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang, Fu) can be resolved, since it is my main alternative.
statement.conflict_note: Unchanged from round 1. I spent a year in John Hall's laboratory in Boulder during my PhD, and Jun Ye is associated with the JILA environment of Hall (from general knowledge, not from my profile). I have not collaborated with Ye or Katori, and I see no recusal requirement, but the committee may note it. I am on the executive management team of WACQT, which overlaps institutionally with Chalmers, Johansson's home. The chair asked whether these need committee handling: I think disclosure in the record is sufficient, and I will abide by whatever the committee decides.
